arc-1-the-bus-ride:
Arc 1: The Bus Ride (Chapters 1–8)

Story Arcs Home · The Birthday Night and Its Aftermath →

Spoiler note: This page covers Chapters 1 to 8. If you are reading along, read it after you finish Chapter 8.

Overview

Vera rides the Grey Goose bus through the Midwest mist toward What Cheer, Iowa. Between stretches on the bus, her memory supplies the two women who shaped her: her opium-dreaming mother, Catherine, and the plain nursemaid Miss MacIntosh, whose disappearance set her traveling. Then the bus takes over: Moses at the wheel, Madge and Homer and their hometown dead, flooded roads, and arrival in a village at night.

Central figures: Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Madge Capehorn · Moses Hunnecker · Catherine Cartwheel · Homer Capehorn

Chapter by chapter

Chapter 1

Vera Cartwheel rides a Grey Goose bus through the mist of the American Midwest. The driver, Moses Hunnecker, has long bushy hair. He whistles, drinks openly from a whiskey bottle, calls on God and the angels, and drives erratically. Vera imagines a wife and children waiting for him at home, then wonders whether she has invented them. The only other passengers are a sleeping couple, Madge and Homer Capehorn. Madge is pregnant and seems to resent it, and Homer sleeps in placid innocence. Along the roadside Vera sees a moving van piled with furniture and a double-headed man staring into nothing. These sights lead her to reflect that individuality is an illusion and every soul is joined to every other. She explains why she is traveling. She is searching for Miss MacIntosh, the plain, red-haired nursemaid from What Cheer, Iowa, who disappeared or died. She was the one solid presence in Vera's childhood, in a house by the New England sea ruled by her mother's opium dreams.

Chapter 2

Vera describes her mother, Catherine. She is an opium addict who has lain in bed for years among jewels and phantoms and treats her hallucinations as more real than the world. The chapter traces how she came to this. There was a brief marriage to Jock Cartwheel, and a love triangle with twin brothers: Catherine loved Peron Spitzer, who did not love her, while his brother Joachim loved Catherine without return. Joachim, Mr. Spitzer, is the family lawyer and visits her bedside every evening. An Egyptian sailor arrives looking for the dead Peron and mistakes Joachim for him, and Catherine gives the sailor elaborate directions through her labyrinthine house. There is also the chauffeur, James, with whom she once tried to run away. Whenever her canary dies, Mr. Spitzer secretly replaces it. The chapter ends when a canary escapes into a thunderstorm. Catherine calmly accepts that she must now live forever and dismisses its distant twittering as another dream.

Chapter 3

After Catherine took to her bed, Mr. Spitzer hired Miss Georgia MacIntosh of What Cheer, Iowa, to raise Vera. Vera paints her in full: marcelled red hair, a broken nose, a black umbrella, a tight corset, sensible shoes, morning swims in any weather, strict schedules, and a deep suspicion of anything imaginary. She is everything Catherine is not, the practical Middle West in one person. Vera recalls how Miss MacIntosh dealt with an Australian bushman living in the household who was obsessed with her head, and she mentions the nursemaid's brother. Then Vera returns to the loss. Miss MacIntosh's clothes were found on the beach and her purse held two pennies. Her body was never found, and Vera blames herself. Mr. Spitzer always insists that she was a good and dependable woman who never wavered.

Chapter 4

For years after the disappearance, Vera grieves by the shore. Her hair is cropped and her body heavy, and she drifts in sleep and dreaming. She tries to write a book, lights fires on the beach, and questions fishermen and sailors. Catherine decides her daughter is losing her mind and offers the only cure she knows: opium and a dreamless paradise of eternal youth. Vera refuses and leaves for What Cheer by way of Grand Central Station. She recalls a young woman who jumped from the Brooklyn Bridge in her wedding veil on her way to be married. On the train, a fat, soft-faced lady warns her that the Middle West is desolate, a place of old people who are deaf because they do not wish to hear.

Chapter 5

Night falls on the bus. The roads are flooded and there are no stars or signposts. The bus waits at a Pennsylvania Railroad crossing while Madge moans in her sleep, accusing every man but her husband. Moses sings, drinks, and holds forth. He refuses ever to cut his hair. He rails against the Democrats and the New Deal, though he never has time to vote. He lives with his old mother, has never married, and talks constantly of pregnant women and of old Doc O'Leary, who once delivered babies and has now lost his mind. Birth and death fill his talk. The chapter leaves open whether Moses is driving the bus or only dreaming that he drives it.

Chapter 6

The bus passes broken gates, fallen pillars, and a derelict windmill in a flooded field. Madge wakes and her story emerges. She is five months pregnant, older than Homer, and worked as an operator in a pottery town. She married Homer to give her child a father, though the real father is a man named Adam. Homer, half asleep, dreams of his high school sweetheart, Jacqueline White, who is dying of tuberculosis. Madge accuses him of loving her still, and he denies it. Death runs through both families. Madge's mother died giving birth to her. Years later her father mistook Madge for her dead mother, ran into a winter storm, and drowned. Homer's father killed himself when he learned his wife was pregnant. Madge expects to die in childbirth. The chapter ends with her painting her lips in a darkened mirror and finding she has painted two mouths.

Chapter 7

Through rain and flood, Moses spots the wheelless frame of old Doc's Model T by the road. He imagines the doctor tending patients who are ghosts or were never born. He mocks the old man and is moved by him, but does not stop. Inside the bus, Madge tells Homer the dark stories of their hometown. Josh and Rudolph Hathaway were brothers, and both are dead. Gertrude, who married first one and then the other, is accused by Madge of killing them both, in a murky story of a locked door and a fire. Musidora, Gertrude's simple-minded sister, was married off to an old man and has too many children, who play in the graveyard. Homer wants to think the best of everyone. Madge brings the talk back to Jacqueline, and Homer says he is hungry.

Chapter 8

The bus pushes through a cloudburst with a broken windshield wiper, the road barely distinguishable from the flooded fields. It stops at a fork near a hill of old tombstones, beside Beatrice Fitzgerald's tin house in a yard of mud and wreckage. Madge calls Beatrice a common prostitute. Homer defends her: a hard worker who lost an eye to a boy's arrow, whose son, rumored to be old Doc's, joined the Navy. Moses delivers a long, dark meditation on death and medicine, insisting that no doctor could have saved Jacqueline. The bus enters a village at night. Its houses look like coffins under a skull-like moon, and Vera wonders whether she has arrived in a land of eternal night or a dream within a dream.

arc-3-mr-spitzer:
Arc 3: Mr. Spitzer (Chapters 25–29)

← The Birthday Night and Its Aftermath · Story Arcs Home · Cousin Hannah →

Spoiler note: This page covers Chapters 25 to 29. If you are reading along, read it after you finish Chapter 29.

Overview

A portrait of Mr. Spitzer: Peron's fall from a window, the glass wall and the clerk who declared him dead, his law practice among the dead, the two watches, and his abandoned butterflies, which become a meditation on death, resurrection and the soul.

Central figures: Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah

Chapter by chapter

Chapter 25

Vera considers Mr. Spitzer, whom Catherine accuses of being dead, or of being his own dead brother. We learn how Peron died. He fell through a fourteenth-floor window, perhaps by suicide, perhaps mistaking the window for a door. Joachim himself once walked through a glass wall in another lawyer's office without noticing, and his valet later found glass behind his ears. Bills for the wall followed. When Joachim finally tried to collect damages for his discomfort, a clerk told him that Mr. Spitzer had died several years ago.

Chapter 26

Mr. Spitzer's field of law is the dead: wills, deeds, archives, and lost heirs. One case involves two Boston spinsters, each believing she is Cleopatra. One left her fortune to her Siamese cats under his supervision, and the cats seem likely to live forever. He asks what Peron would have done had their places been reversed. He concludes that Peron would never have been faithful to Catherine's bedside, but would have dragged her into the living sunlight even if it killed her. He reflects that to reach the upper world one must first travel through the lower.

Chapter 27

Vera grows exasperated with the adults who circle their problems endlessly. Mr. Spitzer carries calling cards and an old passport so that, if he is found dead, he will be identified as himself and not his brother. He wears Peron's accurate wristwatch, and has lately rediscovered his own identical watch, broken and stopped near the time of Peron's death, and wears it too. He is always late and always caught between streams of traffic. A stranger once asked him on a crowded street whether he wanted to die. He said no while nodding yes, and was led safely across.

Chapter 28

Mr. Spitzer admits that he may be only another of Catherine's hallucinations, and that he truly lives only during these evenings in her room. He recalls the butterfly collection he abandoned after Peron's funeral, his correspondence with fellow collectors, and the births and deaths of butterflies he watched. If one were called away at the crucial moment, he observes, one could never tell whether one had seen a beginning or an end.

Chapter 29

Mr. Spitzer speaks at length about butterflies. He compares the difficulty of telling butterfly from moth to telling brother from brother, and happiness from sorrow. He names species by the hundreds and dwells on the butterfly as psyche, the soul. He describes Peron's funeral, crowded with gamblers and merry mourners, and the one person who saw his grief, an old lamplighter weeping on a street corner. He wonders whether a sock darned again and again until no original thread remains is still the same sock. The chapter ends with him as a dark atheist who knows more of the life beyond the grave than of this one.
arc-8-esther-longtree:
Arc 8: Esther Longtree (Chapters 72–81)

← The Tavern · Story Arcs Home · The Ending →

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. Chapter 74, with its account of rape, is especially difficult.

Spoiler note: This page covers Chapters 72 to 81. If you are reading along, read it after you finish Chapter 81.

Overview

At the Greasy Spoon, Vera listens to Esther Longtree, the everlastingly pregnant waitress: her stillborn children, the fathers, the Chicago detective, the mud baby, her twin Rosemary, her strange conception, Walter, and the little toy salesman.

Central figures: Esther Longtree · Vera Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Justice O’Leary · Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh

Chapter by chapter

Chapter 72

On an early spring morning, Vera enters the Greasy Spoon, between the undertaker's and the beauty parlor, and meets Esther Longtree. She is a big, crossed-eyed waitress with a bald spot, a deformed foot, and a belly swollen for as long as anyone remembers. She believes she is always pregnant, now with "the little shadow boxer," whose two hearts she can feel. His fathers were traveling salesmen. Dr. O'Leary once called her the immortal medical case. She ponders who killed Cock Robin and answers that everyone and no one did.

Chapter 73

Esther describes her stillborn children as fragments: an eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb, a snowflake. She hid them in streams, snow, and tree stumps, and the undertaker complains she brings him no business. Dying fathers write to ask whether their child lived, and she keeps their illusions intact. A Chicago detective circles her, and she fears arrest. The story of the boxer Joe Goldberg enters her tale.

Chapter 74

Esther dreads a trial before a jury. The Chicago detective has come three times in three disguises, collecting clues for murders no one else notices. He is also the man who raped her. He cares only about the deaths of white children. Esther's speech begins to repeat words in threes, and she hints at an old, hidden death from her youth. Her own childhood reproaches her.

Chapter 75

Vera listens to Esther all morning, perhaps through many mornings. Esther wonders whether she carries a child or a tumor. The detective returns and accuses her of murdering his children. She tells of the mud baby, which she and a fisherman wrapped in a sack and threw into the river, and which returns in dreams, larger in death and hung with a funeral wreath. A darker suspicion about its father hovers unspoken. She hopes the coming war will make old murders seem small.

Chapter 76

Esther wonders whether her successful conceptions were her worst mistakes. The detective solves every mystery except his own. She says she killed her twin sister in the womb, and she recalls a story of twin brothers, one of whom murdered the other. She was fired from teaching school on false charges. She begins to welcome the trial, though she will answer only her own questions, and she is tired of all the men and all the fathers.

Chapter 77

Esther asks who killed the heavens and the earth and love itself. The detective sends her an old clipping about a mass murderess, an abortionist who killed unmarried mothers and their newborns. She was caught after killing a woman who was pregnant only in her dreams. Esther reveals that her first child was fathered by a Black man, which makes the detective's indifference to Black children personal. Sterile salesmen keep sending gifts for babies who may be dead.

Chapter 78

Esther was called Little Jackass from birth, because she was born kicking and stubborn. Her tiny, cold mother blamed her for the stillbirth of her twin, Rosemary, the perfect child, saying Esther kicked her out of the womb. Esther grew up lonely, often tied to a tree in the yard. Her father was a large, timid policeman who patrolled the graveyard to warn off lovers rather than arrest them. She wonders whether she herself is the shadow, the one who never truly lived.

Chapter 79

Esther's parents never consummated their marriage. For seven years a large, dark woman in men's clothes came to their house at night with a tiny silver spoon, until Esther and Rosemary were conceived. An uncle, a boxer, told her the story, laughing. On her seventh birthday, Esther's mother took her to visit the dying, blind go-between, and Esther saw in her the father she never had. Ever since, every day has been her birthday.

Chapter 80

Esther makes tiny clothes for no one and sets out crumbs for spirits. She tells of her first child, Walter. His father was a Black man who had escaped a lynching and came to her one night, then fled. Alone and frightened, she gave birth and pressed her thumb to still Walter's cry. Believing she had killed him, she hid him and ran. Yet she imagines him alive and growing somewhere, returning in visions to ask why she killed him and where his father is.

Chapter 81

On a rainy day, Esther hopes to marry at last. She remembers the little toy salesman: childlike, nearly toothless, drinking milk from a baby bottle, the son of a famous spy mother and a window-peeping father. He was the sole survivor of a shipwreck, drifting in a rubber lifeboat past the drowned while a shark circled. He told her the bad men would blow up the world one calm day, just for fun. She considers marrying him so the little shadow boxer will have a legal father, though she can no longer say who fathered him.
arc-4-cousin-hannah:
Arc 4: Cousin Hannah (Chapters 30–52)

← Mr. Spitzer · Story Arcs Home · Mr. Spitzer's Grief →

Spoiler note: This page covers Chapters 30 to 52. If you are reading along, read it after you finish Chapter 52.

Overview

Catherine's memories summon Cousin Hannah, the suffrage captain, and with her Catherine's own spectral marriage and the architecture of her opium mind. The arc then moves to Hannah's deathbed and its long aftermath, as Mr. Spitzer, her executor, pieces together a hidden life, finds the trunks of wedding gowns, and keeps her secret. Volume One ends at Chapter 50.

Central figures: Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer

Chapter by chapter

Chapter 30

Catherine and Mr. Spitzer discuss unreal persons as if they were real, especially Eustace, an invisible visitor who takes many shapes. Then Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden enters through memory. She was a Boston suffragette, archer, duelist, climber, and traveler who crossed deserts disguised as an Arab king, and she seemed to foresee assassinations. She is now dead and buried. She never cared for the Spitzer twins. Catherine longs for her company and imagines sending her to search the Alps for Jock, Catherine's husband, who vanished while mountain climbing.

Chapter 31

Catherine and Mr. Spitzer admire Cousin Hannah, whose great deeds made their own lives seem unfulfilled. Her secret grief is circled but never named: the mirrors of her house draped in black, her failed battle to rescue Catherine from opium, her indifference to both Spitzer brothers. Mr. Spitzer remembers his long faithfulness to her, knocking at a door that never opened. He struggles to write her epitaph, drafting and discarding version after version.

Chapter 32

Catherine remembers Hannah as a storm of a woman with a saber scar and burning eyes, who tried to break up Catherine's wedding by beating the bridegroom with her white umbrella and carrying the bride away. Catherine's marriage itself is spectral: a faceless bridegroom, a wedding to a sailboat, a porpoise, a star, a church bell. Hannah died old and alone and never married, though Catherine believes she still visits. Catherine always wanted to die while traveling, believing that death comes from partial knowledge.

Chapter 33

A Boston newspaper once referred to Catherine as "the late Mrs. Catherine Cartwheel," and Mr. Spitzer never told her. The same paper reported Peron seen walking on Benevolent Street, and Mr. Spitzer walked there the next evening. Catherine cannot remember her wedding or her groom, and sometimes thinks she married Death in her sleep. Mr. Spitzer decides that her dreaming is no farther from reality than the routines of people who punch clocks. The chapter ends with him rising to open a door she has asked a human-sized blackbird to open.

Chapter 34

Catherine recalls being married both in white and in black, with a dog reciting the ceremony in Latin and a St. Bernard giving her the last sacrament. Then she remembers Hannah's presence in her room: iron keys at her belt, a metallic energy, sharp wit, contempt for mortal men, and total indifference to Mr. Spitzer. In Hannah's company Catherine felt both flirtatious and guilty, sensing a love she could not name. Hannah always predicted that Joachim would fail Catherine at the crucial moment, as Peron had by his suicide.

Chapter 35

Catherine imagines inviting Hannah back for a winter of card games. She reviews Hannah's suffrage career on every front, her conquests and her refusal of any memorial window, and all the things Hannah was not: no dancer, no hostess, no keeper of private confessions. She concludes that Hannah was married to the suffrage movement as if it were her husband. Mr. Spitzer notes Catherine's habit of always taking the opposite view.

Chapter 36

Catherine wants to know exactly where Hannah is now. Since she lives among both the living and the dead, she sees no reason she should not be told. She blames Mr. Spitzer, the last person to see Hannah alive, for his useless vagueness. Roused for once, he accuses Catherine of never having loved any living being. Catherine wonders whether Hannah is a man or a woman on the other side, and suspects she would turn heaven to chaos within a week.

Chapter 37

Vera describes the world as Catherine experiences it: drifting mirrors, ceilings that become floors, clocks striking impossible hours. She asks who the dreamer is. Catherine declares that order is a madman's dream. She still schemes to bring Hannah back, but Hannah will not return. Death has throttled her, and silence follows.

Chapter 38

Catherine's memories of Hannah are vague and clouded by her dreams of an immortal love. She has reinterpreted Peron's neglect as a devotion too large to express. We learn that Catherine never believed in women's suffrage, the cause of the woman who tried hardest to save her. Mr. Spitzer adds his anecdotes, and Hannah appears in memory with keys and jeweled sword. Vera names the house for what it has become: a loony bin by the sea.

Chapter 39

Ironically, Hannah the rationalist became for Catherine a figure of dead romance. Vera maps her mother's mind as an infinite house, visited by figures such as Lord Murdock Burdock Thrushmorton and Mr. Res Tacamah. Catherine admits that opium has poisoned her pleasures at their source. Vera describes their meeting as "the perpendicular pronoun I" coming to see "my horizontal mother." The chapter ends asking whether God, too, dreams opium dreams, and whether dream and reality are the same.

Chapter 40

Catherine remembers Hannah's voice, a husky baritone like iron bells, which seemed to speak every language of the living and the dead. In Catherine's mind time runs backward and sideways, her many selves wander the house, and the living and the dead mingle freely. Mr. Spitzer watches from the edge of the room. The chapter closes with Catherine's belief that a ship's figurehead knows more than its captain, because it always goes first.

Chapter 41

Catherine believes only a hair's breadth separates life from death. Her selves leave her body and may not return, furniture drifts, and windows face different seas. She imagines herself an engineer, a builder of cities, a traveler across deserts, yet she cannot walk. Mr. Spitzer complains that she never saw him as a unique person, and so he never learned who he was. Catherine does not envy Hannah's single, steady purpose.

Chapter 42

Catherine rides in a glass carriage behind four alabaster horses, driven by the black coachman, through the sleeping house toward Hannah's deathbed. Mr. Spitzer, a keeper of lists of lost ships, keeps vigil beside the dying suffragette. He finds her crippled, wrapped in an old army coat, sobbing and delirious in a white tent of a room. He wonders what her battles truly won, and she cries out to be hidden from the eyes of men.

Chapter 43

In silk hat and black cape, Mr. Spitzer keeps watch, unsure whether he himself is living or dead. Hannah's dying becomes a dance of death. She raves through deserts, mountains, and snow, speaks to Caesar, a blacksmith, and a figure she calls her love, asks for a mirror, and longs for silk skirts and parasols she scorned all her life. She asks whether she is the anvil or the hammer, and at the end she cries out for a lost beloved under the snow.

Chapter 44

Over the years, Mr. Spitzer pieces together fragments of Hannah's hidden life from her papers: letters, unreadable languages, evidence of a double existence. He recalls her deathbed talk of skirts and petticoats, strange from the great champion of bloomers, and her cry that false modesty killed her love. He wonders whether heroes are driven by a secret cowardice, and whether those who never loved know most of love.

Chapter 45

Reading Hannah's faded letters by candlelight, Mr. Spitzer vows to keep her great secret until long after her death. He sees that her public and private lives cannot be fitted into one portrait. He recalls her asking whether she was always falling, and her sense that she aspired higher and so fell farther. He considers what her grave should say, and how public memory turns the greatest lives into monuments and loses the secret heart.

Chapter 46

Mr. Spitzer realizes that Hannah was also a secret mountain climber, of peaks real and of the mind. As her executor he takes her alpenhorn for his collection of instruments. He wanders a fog-bound city asking strangers whether they have seen her, and people take him for mad. A steeplejack answers him in paradoxes. The chapter ends with Hannah's last cry to the bright star of her love.

Chapter 47

Mr. Spitzer remembers Hannah's last words about the mountains moving, and lays her skirt over her body. He wonders whether her love was that skirt, covering her wound. He reflects on what he owes his twin, on materialism and spirit, on everything in the world seeming conscious, and on the rejected possibility, the life that was never lived. He decides it is better that lost things sink whole than drift scattered.

Chapter 48

In Hannah's house of whispering sounds and keys that fit no lock, Mr. Spitzer performs his duties as a messenger of the dead. He contrasts Peron, who burned brightly and lit matches, with himself, who always feared catching fire. He imagines himself a lamplighter of the stars and is jealous of anyone who might take his place. He sees life as a long rehearsal for the silence.

Chapter 49

In the longest of his meditations, Mr. Spitzer moves through a frozen cosmos of the mind. He mourns Martha, the last passenger pigeon, who died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1918, weeping for others who did not weep for him. He lists the contradictions of his existence, dying through life and living through death. He wonders whether he is one man or two, bound so closely to his brother that he cannot tell which he is.

Chapter 50

The universe seems off key to Mr. Spitzer: two golden chairs where there should be one, his life a dream dreamed by someone else, himself a blank page between testaments. He considers what he absorbed from Catherine and concludes that "all that happened happened only once." He thinks of Hannah's hyphenated name, Freemount-Snowden, and how the hyphen joining the two names mattered more to her than either name. He writes a nocturne for her. Volume One ends.

Chapter 51

A mouse has gotten into Mr. Spitzer's papers, eating his chords and nesting in old lawsuits. Mr. Spitzer catalogs the selves he might be: the trumpeter or the trumpeter's cry, a conductor, a lamplighter, a lawyer to starfish, a man who has stamped documents with the wrong seals for years. In his wanderings he meets people lost in their own illusions, such as a woman who believes she is a birdcage. He concludes that every dream of life must leave something unrealized, or all would be complete.

Chapter 52

Going through Hannah's estate, Mr. Spitzer opens trunk after trunk of wedding gowns, with no bride's slippers among them. He finds letters in languages he cannot read, her lost skirt embroidered with forget-me-nots, and evidence that she lived as Hannah in Boston and as Hamid in the East. Her book lies open to the tale of Tristram and Iseult. He resolves to keep her secret. He closes her eyes and weights them with two pennies, one for the sun and one for the moon.

Arc 2: The Birthday Night and Its Aftermath (Chapters 9–24)

← The Bus Ride · Story Arcs Home · Mr. Spitzer →

Spoiler note: This page covers Chapters 9 to 24. If you are reading along, read it after you finish Chapter 24.

Overview

Vera returns to her childhood under Miss MacIntosh: the lessons, the empty fourteenth birthday party, the dream wedding. On the birthday night she wanders the gardens and the shore, rides Falada into the house, and finds Miss MacIntosh bald and changed. A long night and a silent pact follow, then the breakfast-table days in which nothing may be said, and Vera's survey of a household with no one to guide her.

Central figures: Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Peron Spitzer · Cousin Hannah

Chapter by chapter

Chapter 9

Vera asks whether she caused Miss MacIntosh's death simply by opening her eyes. She recalls their life together: drills in geography and history, the Chicago fire and the glaciers, embroidery hoops and hemmed handkerchiefs, Solomon the turtle dragging a geranium pot across the schoolroom, and the silver dollar watch Miss MacIntosh used to remind her that time was passing. Then comes her fourteenth birthday. Mr. Spitzer sends a party dress, but no guests come. Vera dances alone and declares she is dancing with Death, and Miss MacIntosh sternly corrects her. That night Vera lies awake wondering about the man she might marry and whether a true marriage could ever be dissolved.

Chapter 10

Unable to picture her own wedding, Vera imagines other weddings and drifts into a dream of one. Mr. Spitzer is the veiled bride and Miss MacIntosh the bridegroom. The preacher's marriage vows slide into a funeral service before he vanishes. Vera wakes troubled rather than amused. She realizes she has been thinking unkindly of Miss MacIntosh as colorless and unwanted, and she feels pity for a woman who gave her life to duty. She is hungry and wants to go to her, but she has been warned not to wander the house or the shore at night.

Chapter 11

In this very short chapter, Vera wonders how she will endure her isolation. She cannot live like her mother, and she trusts herself to know where dream ends and reality begins, as Miss MacIntosh taught her. Meanwhile Catherine works through her alphabet of phantom guests, the P's, Q's, and R's: Pericles, Admiral Peary, Penelope's web, the Pleiades, and Sir Walter Raleigh, who removes his head along with his plumed hat. Mr. Spitzer, as always, has missed it all.

Chapter 12

It is after ten at night, and Vera lies beside the Big Ben alarm clock, the one reliable clock in a house of stopped clocks. Restless, she slips out into a garden her grandfather planted for his blind wife, made to be touched and smelled rather than seen. She moves through it with closed eyes in near ecstasy and meditates on Miss MacIntosh and all she taught. The chapter closes on Catherine's suspicion that Mr. Spitzer sometimes imagines himself to be his dead brother, betting on phantom horses he could know nothing about.

Chapter 13

Vera announces in advance that on this night of her fourteenth birthday she will lose her last certainty. Miss MacIntosh will become a stranger in her eyes, though she does not yet say how. She wanders the garden of the deaf, where life-sized chessmen move on a board of light and shadow among statues and gargoyles. The chapter then turns to Catherine and Mr. Spitzer. Catherine insists that the ear and the heart are dead, that sound has fled the universe, and that this is why his music is silence.

Chapter 14

Vera comes to the grave of the black coachman, who once drove her grandfather's carriage with four white horses. Catherine is obsessed with that grave and its location. She questions Mr. Spitzer endlessly about the coachman's burial and the fate of the horses. Beneath this obsession, the story of the Spitzer twins comes out. Peron fell from a tall building, probably by suicide. Joachim has lived in the aftermath ever since, wearing his brother's cufflinks and being mistaken for him in the street. Catherine goes on talking long after Mr. Spitzer has left, asking about the grave of the other Mr. Spitzer, the one she loved, until dawn puts her to sleep.

Chapter 15

Still on her birthday night, Vera stands by a roaring sea under a skull-white moon. Exhilarated, she runs into the surf. For the first time she looks at Miss MacIntosh critically: what she does not know of undertow and the deeper things, her umbrella carried indoors, her windows thrown open in winter, her bare cold bedroom, the day's long lecture of proverbs about death, marriage, and industry. The sea briefly becomes a vision of the end of time and then goes dark again. Far off, the old blind sheep dog barks at the waves.

Chapter 16

Vera rides her old black pony, Falada, through the dark grounds, laughing and whispering secrets into his ear. She decides not to bring a real horse into her mother's dream-filled bedroom. Instead she rides him up the stairs of the great house, past mosaic emperors, a funeral gondola, and tapestries of angels healing the blind and the deaf. They reach Miss MacIntosh's door, always barred from inside, and it swings open. In the moonlight Miss MacIntosh stands by the window, greatly changed, unbelievably not herself, and yet Vera recognizes her instantly.

Chapter 17

Miss MacIntosh is bald, her skull gleaming like an ivory ball in the moonlight. Vera, shocked and half triumphant, cries out that she is a man. A struggle follows, real or partly imagined. Vera is knocked down, lifted, and laid on the bed, and drifts in and out of consciousness, wondering whether she is wrestling a dummy, a gladiator, or the angel Jacob met. In the morning her braids are neatly plaited, and the only scratches on her cheeks could have come from leafless branches.

Chapter 18

Through the rest of the night, Miss MacIntosh holds Vera and talks. She speaks in two voices: the familiar one of proverbs and common sense, and a raw, grieving one that cries about the breast she lost and the hair that was never hers. She insists nothing happened. She scolds Vera for entering without knocking and threatens to kill her if she tells. By dawn she is quizzing her on geography again. As Vera falls asleep, Miss MacIntosh whispers that she lost her hair in Vera's service, that she once had a pale gold mane, and that she is not as old as Vera thinks.

Chapter 19

Vera wakes at dawn in Miss MacIntosh's bed, half hoping the night was a dream. Before opening her eyes she reconsiders details she never questioned: the baseball cap, the evening ribbons, the veils over the whaler's hat, the umbrella indoors. Then she looks. The bald head lies on the pillow. The red wig hangs on the hat rack. Around the bare room are false teeth in a glass, a Bible chained to the table, a deuce of clubs, cards printed with Dutch windmills, and seaweed hanging on the barred door. Then she sees that one breast has been amputated.

Chapter 20

In full dawn Vera studies the sleeping woman, thinking about God, about hair, and about what the night revealed. She makes her decision: she will act as though she never saw. She will iron the shirts more eagerly, learn the genealogies and ancient measures, and keep the secret. She will protect Miss MacIntosh from the knowledge of herself. The chapter ends in a litany of biblical images for God.

Chapter 21

Vera takes a last long look at Miss MacIntosh asleep: the scar, the missing eyebrows and lashes, a green ribbon looped over a bust of Martin Luther. She falls back asleep. When she wakes, Miss MacIntosh stands fully dressed, her red wig shining, in unusually good humor, and the room is tidy as if nothing happened. She says Vera has been sick and scolds her for dancing without a partner. She holds up the birthday dress Mr. Spitzer sent, declares it cannot be mended, and sends it to the ash bin.

Chapter 22

At an unusually festive breakfast of fine china and white roses, Miss MacIntosh reads the newspaper aloud: rebellions, Wall Street, storms, strikes, the price of eggs. She fires questions at Vera, complains about dust and unmatched socks, and talks about shipwrecks off the coast. Vera is irritated by her cheerfulness, asks twice about the ruined dress, and is deflected. Almost in passing, Miss MacIntosh remarks that baldness is no cure for sorrow. Vera begins to wonder whether her nursemaid is as dreamlike as everyone else.

Chapter 23

The breakfast continues. Miss MacIntosh denounces vain man, the Emperor Constantine, and Caesar, declares that history lies, and professes her faith in common sense and the middle way. Then she settles on Benjamin Franklin, whose experiments with lightning led to electric light and the end of privacy. Darkness, she argues, once protected marriage and the poor and the ugly. Vera realizes what the tirade is for: a woman who was just seen without her wig is arguing that no one should have to be seen. The chapter ends with Miss MacIntosh quoting Job and crying that the stars have always lit the heavens.

Chapter 24

Vera's thoughts move through the household. The servants have absorbed Catherine's dreams so completely that they argue whether it is Roman in the morning and Greek in the afternoon, and assign rooms to famous phantom guests. Catherine plans her own funeral, calls Athens on a telephone wired only to the servants' quarters, and tries to reach Cousin Hannah on a number long disconnected. Mr. Spitzer will come again in the evening with his vague certainties about heaven. Vera asks herself to whom she can turn with her questions about love, marriage, birth, and death, and finds no one.

Arc 5: Mr. Spitzer's Grief (Chapters 53–62)

← Cousin Hannah · Story Arcs Home · Miss MacIntosh's Last Month →

Spoiler note: This page covers Chapters 53 to 62. If you are reading along, read it after you finish Chapter 62.

Overview

Mr. Spitzer and his twin: their opposite natures, the mirrored house, the funeral and its debts, the tailor's bill that will not stop, and his wanderings among street musicians, a silent violinist, wild ducks and a mute who loses his frog, ending in a will that leaves his music to the world.

Central figures: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Cousin Hannah · Vera Cartwheel · Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh

Chapter by chapter

Chapter 53

No instrument is wide enough for Mr. Spitzer's feelings. He contrasts Peron, a chameleon of many colors, with himself, a timid chess player who never made the final move. Since the death he has been mistaken for his brother and has come to know things only Peron knew: boxing records, gambling, speakeasies. He calls himself a pale replica, divided between himself and his twin.

Chapter 54

From his years with Catherine, Mr. Spitzer knows the underworld of dreams. He wanders a Boston whose buildings keep rearranging themselves. He helps derelicts and lost heirs, and is troubled by an old accusation that he stole a rajah's jewel. He prefers glass jewels to real ones. The chapter ends with his elegy, written on scraps of paper, blowing away down a dark street while he stands weeping and stamping his cane.

Chapter 55

The twins had opposite mottos: Peron's "carpe diem," seize the day, and Joachim's "hoc opus, hic labor est," this is the work, this the labor. Joachim had planned a quiet life of music and stamp collecting in their twin house of mirrored rooms. Peron borrowed, forged his brother's checks, and left debts. When Peron died, Joachim paid for the funeral and the debts, went bankrupt, and lost the house. He now lives in a beachcomber's shack, still wondering whose funeral it was.

Chapter 56

Mr. Spitzer recalls dressing Peron's body in an elegant black suit cut like his own, and burying him with poker chips, dice, a playing card, and a red rose, while a one-armed violinist and a racetrack bugler played. Over the years he gave Peron's huge wardrobe away to the poor. He doubts reality, wonders who tailored his strange life, and carries a golden key to a door that no longer exists.

Chapter 57

A bill keeps arriving from the tailor who made Peron's funeral suit, though the tailor and his shop cannot be found. Mr. Spitzer follows directions from his dreams and searches city directories in the library. There he meets a Confederate soldier who believes the South won, and readers debating immortality. He imagines a rose named for both brothers, red and white on a single bush.

Chapter 58

On the library steps, Mr. Spitzer meets an old violinist with shaking fingers who plays an imaginary violin. Mr. Spitzer recognizes the silent piece at once, a forgotten minor composition, and hears what is not there. He admits he distinguishes less and less between reality and his dreams, and suspects this may be his only wisdom.

Chapter 59

Mr. Spitzer tosses coins to street musicians and beggars without knowing who is poor or rich, living or dead. His eyesight dims. He considers chance and order and tries to write an equation for the place between life and death. He suspects that the skeleton inside him is not his own, and concludes that everything would be explained if he admitted he was already dead.

Chapter 60

Mr. Spitzer wonders whether he is a musician at all or has really been a gambler, since he reads only the sporting pages. At dusk he practices moose calls in the city, and a moose seems to answer through the fog. Then wild ducks follow him for days, and he decides their cry can be his elegy.

Chapter 61

In a thieves' café, Mr. Spitzer befriends an old mute who has trained a frog in his mouth to speak for him, even to recite the Lord's Prayer. When the frog dies, the two men bury it in an upland meadow, and the walk back seems shorter than the walk there. Mr. Spitzer wonders whether the mute is his ideal audience. He thinks about silence, and about the music he has scattered on scraps across Boston and other cities.

Chapter 62

Mr. Spitzer dreams of rowing down a river that turns from fire to ice. He rewrites his will, leaving his music to the world. He learns the full story of the silent violinist from the library steps, and remembers a clarinetist who killed himself, leaving a note that he was going to join a greater orchestra. Crossing Louisburg Square, he is startled to learn he is in Boston and not Philadelphia.

arc-6-miss-macintoshs-last-month:
Arc 6: Miss MacIntosh's Last Month (Chapters 63–66)

← Mr. Spitzer's Grief · Story Arcs Home · The Tavern →

Spoiler note: This page covers Chapters 63 to 66. If you are reading along, read it after you finish Chapter 66.

Overview

The novel returns to Vera and Miss MacIntosh. The wig comes off, and Miss MacIntosh tells her life: the childhood baldness, the orphans, Lorena, and Mr. Bonebreaker, who fled. Then the last lessons through a storm, and the September morning she walks into the sea.

Central figures: Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Joachim Spitzer · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Catherine Cartwheel · Moses Hunnecker

Chapter by chapter

Chapter 63

The novel returns to Vera and Miss MacIntosh. Vera confronts her about the hollow pretense between them. Miss MacIntosh takes off her wig and speaks more openly than ever about her past, her body, her loneliness, and her coming end. She tells Vera that "nobody knows anybody," and that she suffers especially when there are rainbows.

Chapter 64

Solomon the turtle is missing. Bald and unguarded, Miss MacIntosh tells Vera her life story: childhood baldness, wigs made of stolen horsehair, boys trying to hook her wig with fishing lines, a phrenologist who admired her skull, a Gaelic prince among her ancestors. As a matron of orphans she cared for a forger, who later wrote to her from Alcatraz, and for Lorena, a dancing girl she loved. Vera sees her as she cannot see herself and begins to compose an elegy. Their last month together begins.

Chapter 65

Miss MacIntosh tells Vera about her one romance, with Mr. Titus Bonebreaker, a street preacher from Missouri who proclaimed the end of the world. They were engaged, but when she showed him the truth of her body, he fled, leaving his umbrella behind. She kept it, and the luminous watch he gave her. She worked among the blind in Chicago, where her differences mattered less, and later stood alone on a boat full of honeymooners, resolved to forget him.

Chapter 66

Dressed for a long voyage in whaler's hat and sea boots, Miss MacIntosh teaches Vera through a storm. She fires questions about geography, finance, and the body, describes her imaginary raids on the Stock Exchange, which she calls a palace of evil, and her Arctic explorer, and speaks of her removed ovaries. Then, one cold September morning, she walks into the sea. Her clothes are found on the beach and her red wig is torn in the sand, while old Friday, the sheep dog, barks at the waves.
arc-9-the-ending:
Arc 9: The Ending (Chapter 82)

← Esther Longtree · Story Arcs Home

Spoiler note: This page covers Chapter 82. If you are reading along, read it after you finish Chapter 82.

Overview

Catherine is dead and the house is gone to the sea. Mr. Spitzer's last confession, Vera's new understanding of Miss MacIntosh, and the stone deaf man with whom Vera will marry and make a child.

Central figures: Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Esther Longtree

Chapter by chapter

Chapter 82

Vera thinks of all she could have confessed to Esther. Her mother is dead. The sea swept away the house with its golden towers, leaving chandeliers strewn along the shore, and only the string of pearls she wears remains to her. She is mourning three deaths. At the end, Catherine rose from her bed and walked. Mr. Spitzer carried her into the garden by the sea and declared his love. He told her he was really Peron, and that it was Joachim who had died. But Catherine had already died in his arms before he spoke. He also lost his old valet, the clam-digger, in the storm. Vera sees Miss MacIntosh anew: "Whatever is average is the dream. Whatever is hidden is the revealed." At dawn in the hotel corridor she meets a stone deaf man, who lost his hearing at fourteen. They become lovers, and he whispers that their child will be his ear. They plan to marry and invite everyone, the flowers and birds and Esther Longtree, who hangs a misspelled sign in the restaurant window, "Owt to luntsch. bee bak in a whale."

arc-7-the-tavern:
Arc 7: The Tavern (Chapters 67–71)

← Miss MacIntosh's Last Month · Story Arcs Home · Esther Longtree →

Spoiler note: This page covers Chapters 67 to 71. If you are reading along, read it after you finish Chapter 71.

Overview

The bus reaches Indiana. Madge and Homer walk out of the novel, and Vera spends a sleepless night at the Tavern among the Christian hangman Mr. Weed, Dr. O'Leary raging at the dead Sarah through the wall, and the remembered Mrs. Hogden, before a grey morning of inventory.

Central figures: Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Moses Hunnecker · Justice O’Leary · Mr. Weed

Chapter by chapter

Chapter 67

The bus reaches an Indiana tavern and cannot park between a leaking milk truck and a hearse. Moses curses at old Doc, whom he believes is blocking the space with his ghost car. The passengers rock wearily in their seats. Madge laughs breathlessly, and Homer recalls a fun house of mirrors with no doors, wondering which door Jacqueline found.

Chapter 68

At night the bus finally stops. Vera watches Madge and Homer walk away, never to be seen again. She waits to check into the Tavern, a decaying hotel built in 1827, while the landlord talks at the bar with Mr. Weed, a Christian hangman. Mr. Weed's first wife, Marie, hanged herself from a peach tree for fear of another pregnancy. His second wife, Julia, has the mind of a child. His children play at hanging. He carries a pen given to him by a condemned man, a Jew's harp, and a black poker chip of unknown origin, and he considers himself a humanitarian. No clock strikes.

Chapter 69

Vera's room is marked Fire Escape. It has a corn-husk mattress, a "Forget me not" picture of a church steeple, and a slop jar holding someone else's hair combings. The landlord points out the other guests on the way: Moses, a knitting girl named Tillie, an old woman with enormous canaries, and Mr. Weed's shadow. All night, through the thin wall, old Dr. Justice O'Leary rages at Sarah, his dead sister, lists every disease he knows, and mentions his strangest case, a woman who is always pregnant. Vera finally screams at Sarah to go.

Chapter 70

In the quiet, Vera tells of Mrs. Hogden, whose name keeps shifting and whom Vera admits she never actually saw. Mrs. Hogden sold her Dutch windmill home and arrived at Catherine's house with birdcages, temple bells, and a letter of employment as arithmetic teacher that Catherine denied writing. Lisa Lunde, Catherine's new companion, suspected her at once. Mrs. Hogden lived for months in the abandoned playroom, playing chess against herself. She finally left her wig on a crab at the water's edge and a blackboard message reading "All a's are b's."

Chapter 71

Vera has not slept. She wears her mother's black velvet, meant as Catherine's shroud and never used, along with her lace and her pearls, which Catherine believed multiplied when lost. She thinks of Mr. Weed guarding his children through the night. She enters Dr. O'Leary's room, a clutter of mismatched women's shoes, medical instruments, a Yale diploma, and a calendar twenty years out of date. A woman shouts prejudices on the stairs. The Tavern Landlady, in thick dialect, tells her about everyone in town, including a waitress always expecting a baby. The maid, Tabitha, whispers good morning.

Every character on one staff

All the Darlings

Marguerite Young said the novel has no minor characters, that each one has a complete story. This map draws every character on a single staff of 82 chapters, in the manner of the music diagrams in Boethius’s De institutione musica, where a central column of strings is ringed with arcs that join the notes.

Each loop runs from a character’s first chapter to their last. A character whose whole story sits inside one chapter is a small closed knot tied to that chapter. People Vera remembers coil to the left; people she meets on the road, at the tavern, and in Esther’s diner coil to the right. The staff itself is Vera, the one telling, drawn as a bird, the animal the novel names more than any other.

Spoiler note: The map covers every character’s whole span, including the ending. Tap a loop, knot, or name to light that character’s chapters; each name links to its hub.

    How it maps to Boethius

    Boethius drew the musical scale as a column of strings with arcs looping between them, each arc an interval. Here the strings are chapters and the arcs are lives. Cousin Hannah’s chapters (30 to 52) sit at the exact middle of the book, the place of the mese, the middle string the scale is tuned around. The movements pair off around her in simple ratios: the bus (8 chapters) against its return (16), and Mr. Spitzer (5) against his grief (10), each an octave.

    What the full cast shows

    Exactly half the cast, 48 of 96, are knots: complete stories closed inside one chapter. The bus passengers’ loops open in Chapters 1 to 8 and close when the bus resumes at 67 and 68; the house’s loops open in Chapter 2 and close at 82. And Vera, the staff, goes dark from Chapter 23 to 65 while every other loop passes through the middle without her.

The Story in Time

Story Arcs · Chapter Hubs · Start Here

Spoiler note: This page covers the whole novel, including its ending. If you are reading along, use the diagram for orientation and save the table until you finish the book.

Vera tells the novel from a bus journey across the Midwest, but most of its pages are memory, and some are memory inside memory. This page shows how the telling loops and then puts the events in the order they happened.

How the telling loops

The novel opens on the bus and stays there for eight chapters. At Chapter 9 Vera turns back to the night of her fourteenth birthday. From Chapter 24 her memories move into the house, to Mr. Spitzer’s evenings at her mother’s bedside, and from there into his memories of Cousin Hannah and of his own grief. Only at Chapter 63 does the novel return to Miss MacIntosh, for her last month, and only at Chapter 67 does the bus pull up to the tavern.

■ The present: the bus, the tavern, Esther’s diner · ■ Vera’s memories of Miss MacIntosh · ■ The house: Mr. Spitzer and Cousin Hannah

Two threads break off and resume. The bus story stops after Chapter 8 and picks up at Chapter 67, nearly 60 chapters later. Vera’s memories of Miss MacIntosh stop after the birthday breakfast in Chapter 23 and resume at Chapter 63. When the long middle feels endless, it helps to know that both threads are waiting.

Events in the order they happened

Young rarely gives dates or ages, and the table only states what the novel makes clear. Vera’s age is stated only for the birthday night, but she says the last month came after she had seen Miss MacIntosh’s secret, with autumn just beginning, so she is still about fourteen when Miss MacIntosh disappears. The joy of reading Miss MacIntosh, My Darling isn’t getting to the end; it is living inside the dream.

This is a slow read. One chapter at a time, with no chapters grouped together, from Monday, January 3, 2028 to Sunday, April 28, 2030. Short chapters get one week, longer chapters two, and the longest three. 50 chapters take one week, 26 take two, and 6 take three.

How it works

  • Each chapter has its own post on Substack, 82 in all, going up on the Monday the chapter begins. Discussion takes place in the comments of that post for as long as the chapter runs.
  • Assignments are by chapter, so the plan works with any edition.
  • Each chapter number links to its Chapter Hub, the group’s home base, with links to that chapter in every companion book, its For the Curious entries, and the essays that discuss it.
  • In a two- or three-week chapter, read at whatever pace suits you and use the extra time for the site.

How the site fits each chapter

  • Read the chapter first. The hub summary and the Reading Guide both tell what happens, so they work best as a check afterward.
  • Reading Guide: read “What actually happens,” “What to hold onto,” and “What to watch for as you keep reading.”
  • For the Curious: each chapter has between one and eight entries. The schedule names two to start with, and anyone can pick another to bring to discussion.
  • To All My Darlings research notes: use these for the key passages, symbols, and themes.
  • Life, Love, and Truth: each chapter page ends with “For Reflection” questions, which can serve as discussion prompts.
  • One lens per chapter, rotating: The Eleven Pillars, Woman in Young’s Magnum Opus, Religion, the Intertextual Index, or Comedy. Comedy pages exist for 71 chapters, and the hub lists them when they exist.
  • Site search and “Find on this page” follow one motif across the book, such as butterflies, umbrellas, canaries, wigs, or rain.
  • Story Arc pages, Character Hubs, and Masterclass portraits cover the whole novel. First-time readers should read only the arc Overview when an arc begins and save the rest until the arc ends.
  • With every seventh chapter the group reads one Pillar Crosswalk, eleven in all. At the end of most arcs the group reads a chapter of Exploring Reality and Illusion.

All the Darlings

Every character in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling drawn on one staff of 82 chapters, after the music diagrams of Boethius. The same map sits at the end of the Character Hubs, and The Story in Time sets the same chapters in the order the events happened.

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling

The staff of 82 chapters

Marguerite Young said the novel has no minor characters, that each one has a complete story. This map draws every character on a single staff of 82 chapters, in the manner of the music diagrams in Boethius’s De institutione musica, where a central column of strings is ringed with arcs that join the notes.

Each loop runs from a character’s first chapter to their last. A character whose whole story sits inside one chapter is a small closed knot tied to that chapter. People Vera remembers coil to the left; people she meets on the road, at the tavern, and in Esther’s diner coil to the right. The staff itself is Vera, the one telling, drawn as a bird, the animal the novel names more than any other.

Spoiler note: The map covers every character’s whole span, including the ending. Tap a loop, knot, or name to light that character’s chapters; each name links to its hub.

    How it maps to Boethius

    Boethius drew the musical scale as a column of strings with arcs looping between them, each arc an interval. Here the strings are chapters and the arcs are lives. Cousin Hannah’s chapters (30 to 52) sit at the exact middle of the book, the place of the mese, the middle string the scale is tuned around. The movements pair off around her in simple ratios: the bus (8 chapters) against its return (16), and Mr. Spitzer (5) against his grief (10), each an octave.

    What the full cast shows

    Exactly half the cast, 48 of 96, are knots: complete stories closed inside one chapter. The bus passengers’ loops open in Chapters 1 to 8 and close when the bus resumes at 67 and 68; the house’s loops open in Chapter 2 and close at 82. And Vera, the staff, goes dark from Chapter 23 to 65 while every other loop passes through the middle without her.
